titre: Indiana's Circle Bill, Set Aside Without Being Judged Wrong
accroche: In 1897, the Indiana House unanimously passes a text on the circle. The Senate buries it without ever calling it wrong.
contenu_vulgarise:
We often read that Indiana wanted to fix π at 3 by law. The bill does indeed exist, but it never gives the value 3, it does not utter the word π, and it was not a mathematical error that stopped it.

## A Doctor, a Circle, a Bill

Edwin J. Goodwin, a physician in Solitude, in Posey County, had convinced himself that he had succeeded in squaring the circle: constructing a square with the same area as a given circle. He had copyrighted his method and proposed that Indiana adopt it for its schools royalty-free, the rest of the world having to pay. His county's representative, Taylor I. Record, introduces the text on January 18, 1897, as House Bill 246. During the debate, the Purdue account reports, he will say he knew nothing of its contents and had introduced it at Goodwin's request.

The text is confused. Its second section states that the ratio of the diameter to the circumference is "as five-fourths to four." Four divided by five-fourths gives 3.2, not 3. Petr Beckmann, author of *A History of π*, finds in it claims that contradict elementary geometry and, apparently, contradict each other.

## A Unanimous Vote, Then a Burial

Sent first to the Committee on Canals, also called the Committee on Swamp Lands, then to the Committee on Education, the bill emerges with a recommendation for passage. On February 5, 1897, according to the Purdue account, the House votes for it 67 to 0.

That day, Clarence Waldo, a mathematics professor at Purdue, happens to be at the Capitol on an appropriations matter. He stumbles on the debate, declines the offer made to him to be introduced to Goodwin, and spends the evening "coaching" senators, the word is his.

In the Senate, the text is introduced on February 11, approved the next day by the Committee on Temperance, then ridiculed on the floor for half an hour. Senator Hubbell considers that such a discussion is not worthy of a Senate that costs the state $250 a day. He moves for indefinite postponement, which is carried.

## Two Readings of the Rejection

The official history of the Indiana General Assembly, cited by Purdue, gives the credit to Waldo. The Indianapolis Journal's account, cited from a 1935 article, says something else: no speaker against the bill suggested that its theories were wrong, and all the senators who spoke admitted they did not know their value. According to that newspaper, Hubbell compared the attempt to trying to make water flow uphill: one does not establish a mathematical truth by law.

The two readings add up without merging. In the common version, ignorant legislators want to legislate on π. In the documented version, the House unanimously passes a text it does not understand, and the Senate stops it without refuting it, out of concern for dignity and on a principle that happens to be right. The outcome is the right one; the reasoning that leads to it verifies nothing. Should we trust a rejection that rests on no proof?

repere.texte: Section 2 of Indiana House Bill No. 246 (1897) states that “the ratio of the diameter and circumference is as five-fourths to four,” that is, 4 ÷ 1.25 = 3.2 for the ratio of the circumference to the diameter. The text does not use the word π.
repere.source: House Bill No. 246, Indiana State Legislature, 1897, Wikisource transcription (original source not indicated), section 2

carte.punch: The Indiana House voted a text on the circle, 67 to 0. The Senate never called it wrong.
carte.idee: In 1897, the Indiana House adopts Bill 246 on squaring the circle, 67 votes to 0. It does not fix π at 3: the circumference-to-diameter ratio there is 3.2. The Senate postpones it without any speaker calling it wrong: it judges the matter beneath its dignity.

quiz.question: What does the Indiana Senate's 1897 rejection of the circle bill rest on?
choix: A calculation by the senators showing that the proposed ratio gave a wrong value of π
Speakers who say they do not know the value of the text and judge it unworthy of the Senate
Goodwin's refusal to let the state use his method for free
The written opinion of the governor of Indiana, consulted by the Senate
quiz.explication: According to the Indianapolis Journal, cited by Purdue, no speaker said the theories were wrong and all admitted they did not know their value; Senator Hubbell judged the discussion unworthy of a Senate that costs $250 a day and obtained indefinite postponement. The Senate therefore made no calculation, Goodwin offered free use to Indiana, and no opinion from the governor figures in the account.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What exactly does section 2 of the Indiana bill say about the circumference-to-diameter ratio?
choix: That it is exactly 3, spelled out
That it equals π, with no numerical value given
That it varies with the size of the circle
That it is "as five-fourths to four," that is, 3.2
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Section 2 of the bill states that the ratio is "as five-fourths to four," that is, 3.2, and not 3; the word π never appears in it, and the text does not say either that this ratio would vary with the size of the circle.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who is Clarence Waldo, and what did he do on the day of the House vote?
choix: The governor of Indiana, who vetoed the text
Senator Hubbell, author of the motion to postpone
A Purdue professor, there by chance, who coached senators in the evening
A journalist of the Indianapolis Journal, who covered the debate
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Clarence Waldo, a mathematics professor at Purdue, happened to be at the Capitol on an appropriations matter and spent the evening advising senators, unlike Senator Hubbell, the governor, or a journalist of the Indianapolis Journal.
